theme: Rebuild the Temple; the latter glory will be greater
readingInstruction: Read Haggai 1:1-2:23. Sixteen years after the return, the temple is still unfinished. Haggai’s short messages stir the people to build. Notice the repeated call to “consider your ways.”
settingTheScene: It is 520 BC, the second year of Darius. The foundation of the temple was laid in 536, and then the work stopped. The people built their own houses and left God’s house in ruins. Then Haggai appears, with four messages over about four months. His words are brief, direct, and effective. Within weeks the work resumes. The book is a model of how a prophet can move a people.
observation: “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (1:4).
“Now therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways” (1:5).
“You have sown much, and harvested little… and he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes” (1:6).
“Go up to the hills and bring wood and build the house, that I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified” (1:8).
“And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel… and the spirit of Joshua… and the spirit of all the remnant of the people” (1:14).
“I am with you, declares the LORD” (1:13).
“The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. And in this place I will give peace” (2:9).
“On that day… I will take you, O Zerubbabel… and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you” (2:23).
interpretation:
Haggai’s first message is a question: “Is it a time for you to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” The people had said, “The time has not yet come.” They had excuses. Hard times, opposition, economic pressure. But Haggai shows that their priorities were backward. They had put their own comfort first, and the result was frustration. “You have sown much and harvested little.” When you put God last, even your best efforts leak away. The phrase “consider your ways” appears twice. It is a call to honest reflection.

The remarkable response is that the leaders and people obey. And God’s answer is brief and wonderful: “I am with you.” He stirs up their spirits, and they begin to work, twenty-three days after Haggai’s first word.

A month later, the older people are discouraged, since this temple looks like nothing compared with Solomon’s. Haggai answers: “Be strong… and work, for I am with you.” Then he says, “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.” This was not because of gold, but because of whose presence would fill it. It points to the day when Jesus, the glory of God in flesh, would walk in that temple.

The third message is about holiness: you cannot make unclean things clean by touching the holy. Ritual and obedience cannot be separated. But from this day forward, God promises to bless.

The last message is to Zerubbabel. God will shake the heavens and earth, overthrow the kingdoms, and make Zerubbabel “like a signet ring.” The signet ring was a symbol of authority. In Jeremiah 22:24, Jehoiachin was rejected as a signet ring. Now the line of David is chosen again. Zerubbabel is a sign that God’s promise to David is alive.
connection: Matthew 6:33: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” Hebrews 12:26-28 quotes Haggai 2:6 about the shaking of heaven and earth and the unshakable kingdom. John 1:14: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Matthew 1:12-13: Zerubbabel is in the line of Jesus. 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 says we are God’s temple. Philippians 1:6.
application:
“Consider your ways.” Review how you spend time and money. Is there anything where your own comfort has crowded out God?

Start something you have been postponing for God. Take one small step today.

Take courage from “I am with you” in your work.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to show you where you have put your own house before his.
Ask him to stir your spirit to work for him.
Thank him for the promise that his presence is with you.
